newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean defector reports Kim Jong-il murder plot.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector reports Kim Jong-il murder plot.

text.p: North Korean authorities foiled a plot by cadets at a military academy to assassinate top leader Kim Jong-il in 1995, according to a Pyongyang defector living in Seoul.
The cadets planned to axe Kim to death during a martial arts display, the defector wrote in an article published by South Korea's Nae-woe Press, which monitors North Korea.
But the plot by an underground group of some 200 cadets at Kang Gye Military Academy was uncovered by intelligence agents and the ringleaders were executed, the article said.
The article, carried by local newspapers on Monday, was part of a series put out by the government-funded monitoring agency under the title "Untold Stories of a Pyongyang Woman".
Although the articles are unsigned, a Nae-woe official identified the author as the wife of a former North Korean diplomat who arrived last year.
Kim was due to attend a martial arts performance involving a demonstration of precision axe throwing at the academy in the northern province of Jagang bordering China, the article said.
As part of the show, cadets would hurl axes up to 30 metres (98 feet) to kill insects, it said.

It added that there had been numerous plots since the 1970s to kill former "Great Leader" Kim Il sung, who died in 1994, and his son, Kim Jong-il, who inherited the mantle of leadership without acquiring the titles of state president and general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party.
The plot by the Kang Gye cadets was the "largest ever anti-government incident", the article said without elaborating or offering any source for the account.
No hard evidence has ever emerged about anti-government activities in North Korea, where a vast network of secret police ensure obedience to the Stalinist system.
Western human rights groups say there is a huge population of political prisoners in labour camps, but there is almost no information about how the North Korean gulag operates.
A growing stream of defectors point to simmering disatisfaction among the elite -- including diplomats, airforce pilots and doctors -- with life in the impoverished nation.
Last month North Korea's former top ideologue, Hwang Jang-yop, arrived in Seoul after a flight through Beijing and the Philippines.
